data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Idempotent and safe are distinct: safe means read-only (no server state change), while idempotent means state may change but identical repeated requests yield the same result as a single one. An append-only event log surviving at-least-once delivery requires writers to be idempotent, not safe, because writers must modify state yet retries must not compound.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If RFC 9110 defines 'safe' to include idempotent methods by inclusion (safe \u2282 idempotent), the strict separation breaks.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the log architecture uses single-writer (single-leader) with no retry, idempotency may be unnecessary.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If at-least-once delivery is upgraded to exactly-once via broker-side transactional commits, the writer need not itself be idempotent.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"At-least-once delivery retries writes that may have already succeeded. If the write were merely safe it could not record an event at all (safe = no state mutation). If the write were non-idempotent, each retry would append a duplicate event, corrupting replay determinism. The causal mechanism is deduplication: the writer attaches a stable operation key (or sequence number) so the log's append path can detect a replayed entry and discard it, collapsing the effect of N retries to the effect of one. This transforms a raw append (neither safe nor idempotent) into an effectively idempotent operation. RFC 9110 separates the two precisely along this axis: safe methods are cacheable/prefetchable because they have no side effects; idempotent methods (PUT, DELETE) have side effects but are repeatable.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
